passage:
Last semester, a vocational school started a repair club after teachers noticed unused keyboards and laptops in a storage room. The students wanted to practise technical skills, but the school also hoped to reduce unnecessary purchases. Before touching any device, members recorded its condition and asked a teacher to check whether it was safe to repair. Devices with serious battery damage went to a qualified service provider instead.

At first, the club met only on Fridays. Members soon discovered that successful repair involved more than replacing parts. They had to ask users about the problem, test possible causes, and record what they changed. Rina, a new member, once suggested buying a replacement screen immediately. Her partner asked her to check the cable first. A loose connection turned out to be the real problem, and Rina changed her approach on later jobs.

By the end of the eight-week pilot, the club had examined 30 devices and repaired 18. The report did not claim that every remaining device could be fixed cheaply. Some required unavailable parts, while others needed specialist attention. A teacher warned that the repair count alone could not show total financial savings because students had not recorded every cost.

The school plans to continue the club with better records. Members will log the cost of parts, time spent, and whether repaired devices still work after three months. They will also compare replacement prices. The principal says these details will help the school decide which repairs are worthwhile. For Rina, the main lesson is simpler: careful diagnosis should come before an expensive decision.

passage:
A fictional town is considering a vertical farm inside an unused warehouse. Supporters say that growing crops in stacked layers would use the limited floor space efficiently. They also argue that controlled conditions could make production more predictable. The proposal includes a water-recycling system and deliveries to nearby shops. However, the council has not yet approved the investment.

The project team presented a pilot comparison. For the same weekly quantity of vegetables, the conventional system used 1,000 litres of fresh water and the pilot used 300 litres. These figures describe fresh-water input during the trial. They do not include water used to manufacture equipment. The pilot also required electricity for lamps and pumps, and the team has not published a full cost comparison.

Some residents welcome the possibility of local jobs and shorter delivery routes. Others worry that high equipment costs could make the vegetables too expensive for many families. A farmer outside the town asks whether the council will support existing farms as well. Her question adds a perspective missing from the team's promotional leaflet, which quotes only the project's investors.

The council proposes a second, independently monitored trial before making a final decision. It wants records of electricity, labour, maintenance, and crop losses across different months. It also wants interviews with potential customers. The council explains that a lower water figure is encouraging, but it cannot answer every question about affordability or environmental impact.

The writer supports this cautious approach. A vertical farm may be useful in some urban conditions, but its value depends on the resources it needs and the people it serves. Decisions should follow transparent evidence rather than enthusiasm alone.
